sections.prepared_remarks: Amazon reporting Q1 revenue $155.0 billion, up 9 percent year over year. AWS revenue $26.6 billion, up 21 percent — the reacceleration is real. AWS is underpenetrated relative to enterprise IT spending, and the AI wave is creating new workloads and accelerating existing migrations. Over 65 percent of AI unicorns run on AWS. Our custom Trainium and Inferentia chips are now in their second generation — giving us a cost and performance advantage in AI inference. We see Trainium 2 delivering 40 percent better price-performance versus H100 for LLM inference. Amazon Bedrock has over 100 foundation models — the most of any cloud platform — including our own Nova family. Advertising revenue $3.2 billion, up 24 percent. North America retail margin reached 6.9 percent, up from 5.2 percent a year ago. We are reaching the scale where newer AWS infrastructure improvements are becoming visible in margins — server utilization improvements, more efficient depreciation, and the benefits of proprietary chips are all compounding. Fulfillment and content costs are declining as a percentage of revenue as we optimize delivery networks using machine learning.
sections.financial_highlights: EPS $1.59, operating income $15.3 billion, up 78 percent. AWS operating margin expanded to 37.2 percent. North America retail operating margin 6.9 percent, up 170 basis points year over year. International retail losses narrowed significantly. We had $3.7 billion in free cash flow after $27 billion in capex, primarily AWS infrastructure. We expect Q2 revenue $159 to $164 billion, implying 8 to 12 percent growth. AWS guidance maintained at 17 to 21 percent growth range. We are raising full-year capex guidance to reflect AI infrastructure build — we expect to spend $130 billion in 2025, up from $105 billion last year. advertising growth continues to be structural: our contextual AI ad targeting is delivering 40 percent higher ROAS than keyword-based alternatives. This is the highest-return advertising business in the industry.
sections.qanda_session:
Justin Post: Andy, on AWS — what's driving the sustained acceleration in revenue growth? Is it new AI workloads, mainframe migrations, or something else? And are you seeing customers shift from experimentation to production deployments at scale?

Andy Jassy: Justin, it's all three. The AI wave is creating entirely new compute needs — but mainframe migrations are accelerating faster than we expected. Companies that have been running COBOL on mainframes for 40 years are finding new urgency to modernize before their developer talent pool ages out. Amazon EC2 mainframe re-platforming to our cloud is one of our fastest-growing migration categories right now. We are also seeing containerization of legacy applications accelerating. The shift from experimentation to production is definitely happening — customers are moving from small pilot budgets to enterprise-wide contracts. AWS annual revenue from these enterprise agreements more than doubled year over year. The AI opportunity is larger than we modeled two years ago — companies with successful AI implementations are expanding across the entire enterprise, and they're choosing us because of our enterprise security, compliance, and the breadth of the platform.

Doug Anmuth: Brian, on retail margins — you've gone from near breakeven to 6.9 percent in North America in 18 months. How much is left in the optimization cycle, and how do we think about the margin trajectory over the next 2 to 3 years? Are we approaching a steady state or is there still structural improvement ahead?

Brian Olsavsky: Doug, I've been very careful not to guide specific margin targets, but I'll give you the components. The fulfillment network optimization alone is still in the early innings — our delivery network has grown faster than e-commerce demand, creating excess capacity that is now being absorbed with faster unit growth and improved routing. We still have 40 fulfillment centers targeted for retrofit with robotics in 2025. The regionalization program that moved inventory closer to customers has cut delivery costs by 15 percent as an average. We're also seeing leverage in technology and content as the e-commerce volume scales. The biggest structural improvement ahead is advertising — it's higher margin than retail and it's growing faster than the core e-commerce business. As advertising becomes a larger revenue mix, it pulls the blended margin higher. We see North America retail operating margins reaching 8 to 10 percent in a few years absent major investments.
sections.forward_outlook: Andy Jassy: The structural advantage Amazon has is data and customer trust at scale. Every interaction with a customer generates data that makes our recommendations, logistics, and advertising more efficient. Over 300 million active customers worldwide, Prime has 240 million subscribers. Kuiper satellite internet will expand our addressable market globally, especially in emerging markets where broadband penetration is low. Our pharmacy business is growing 30 percent year over year. Same-day delivery expansion continues — we now offer same-day delivery in 30 US metro areas across 3 million products. We are investing for the long term without compromising the financial model. The combination of AWS, advertising, and retail margin improvement creates the most powerful long-term growth profile in the industry. We're not optimizing for one quarter — we're building a company that will be more valuable in 10 years than today.
